paragraphs.heading: Smooth balls of stars
paragraphs.text: An elliptical galaxy is shaped roughly like a stretched or squashed ball and looks smooth, with almost no features. Edwin Hubble named ellipticals as one of three main classes in his Hubble sequence, alongside spirals and lenticulars, and wrote about them in his 1936 work The Realm of the Nebulae. Together with lenticulars and the related ES galaxies, they belong to the group astronomers call early-type galaxies.

paragraphs.heading: Old, red and quiet
paragraphs.text: Most ellipticals are made of older, low-mass stars. They hold very little gas or dust between their stars, and are short of the gas that new stars are made from. So they form few new stars, have few young stars or open star clusters, and look red. Their stars are on average much older than those in spiral galaxies. They can, however, have short bursts of star formation when they merge with another galaxy.

paragraphs.heading: Shape and motion
paragraphs.text: Unlike flat, orderly spirals, ellipticals are more three-dimensional and have little structure, and their stars circle the center on fairly random orbits. Hubble labelled them by how round their outline looks, with E0 for a round one. He also saw that the label depends on the angle we view a galaxy from, so some E0 galaxies are really elongated. Labels run up to about E7, but since 1966 it has been known that E4 to E7 galaxies are really lenticulars with tilted disks, which measurements of their rotating star disks have confirmed.

paragraphs.heading: From dwarfs to giants
paragraphs.text: Ellipticals vary in size and mass more than any other type of galaxy. Their diameters run from about 3,000 light years to more than 700,000, and their masses from 10⁵ to nearly 10¹³ solar masses. The smallest, dwarf ellipticals, may be no bigger than a typical globular cluster but hold a good deal of dark matter that such clusters lack. The largest galaxies of all are supergiant ellipticals, or cD galaxies, which can hold over one hundred trillion stars and dominate their galaxy clusters.

paragraphs.heading: Where they live
paragraphs.text: Ellipticals make up roughly 10–15% of the Virgo Supercluster's galaxies, and are not the most common type in the universe overall. They tend to be found in galaxy clusters and compact groups, often close to a cluster's center. Every massive elliptical has a supermassive black hole at its center. The black hole's mass closely tracks the galaxy's mass, as shown by links such as the M–sigma relation, which links the black hole's mass to the velocity dispersion of the stars around it.

paragraphs.heading: How they form
paragraphs.text: How ellipticals form is still an open research question. Hubble first guessed that they turn into spirals, which proved false, though gas and small galaxies falling in may build a disk around an existing ball of stars. Early models had them forming in rapid bursts of star birth at high redshifts, whereas later models stress mergers of disk galaxies, and studies find both ideas plausible. Recent work suggests that gas-rich, or wet, mergers can make lower-mass ellipticals that spin fast, while gas-poor, or dry, mergers may build higher-mass ones that spin slowly.
